summary.text: Since a product unequal to \(1\) cannot be taken over an empty set, the associated-prime set is nonempty; for any member \(p\), if \(2n-p\) were composite, its least prime factor would be at most \(\sqrt{2n-p}\le\sqrt{2n}\) and would force \(p\equiv 2n\pmod q\), contradicting the defining modular exclusion. Thus every such complement is prime, so the maximum associated prime exists and together with its complement gives the required Goldbach partition; choosing any member for each \(n\ge3\) also yields the global conclusion.

full_proof.text:
Let \(M\) be a nonnegative integer, and write
\[
r=\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor.
\]
Define \(GB(M)\) to be the following finite set of primes:
\[
GB(M)=\left\{p:\ p\text{ is prime},\quad r<p\leq \frac M2,\quad
p\not\equiv M\pmod q\text{ for every prime }q\leq r\right\}.
\]
Here \(p\leq M/2\) is interpreted with integer division, equivalently \(2p\leq M\). For \(M=0\), set \(GB(0)=\varnothing\). This set is finite because all its elements lie between \(0\) and \(\lfloor M/2\rfloor\).

This is the same Goldbach-association condition as the one stated in the sequence description. Indeed, if \(p\) is a candidate, then \(p>r\). Thus, for every prime \(q\leq r\), we have \(q<p\), and hence \(q\nmid p\), since \(p\) itself is prime. By Euclid's lemma,
\[
q\mid p(p-M)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad q\mid(p-M).
\]
The condition on the right is equivalent to \(p\equiv M\pmod q\). Consequently, saying that no prime \(q\leq\sqrt M\) divides \(p(p-M)\) is equivalent, for these candidates \(p\), to requiring \(p\not\equiv M\pmod q\) for every prime \(q\leq r\).

The sequence is
\[
a(n)=\prod_{p\in GB(2n)}p,
\]
with the usual convention that the product over the empty set is \(1\). For positive \(n\), this is exactly the defining product in A338777; the special convention at \(M=0\) also gives the stated initial behavior but will play no role below, since all relevant \(n\) satisfy \(n\geq3\).

We first prove the key fact on which both conclusions rest.

**Lemma.** If \(p\in GB(M)\), then \(M-p\) is prime.

**Proof.** Membership of \(p\) in \(GB(M)\) gives
\[
p\text{ prime},\qquad r<p,\qquad 2p\leq M,
\]
and
\[
p\not\equiv M\pmod q
\quad\text{for every prime }q\leq r.
\]
Put
\[
d=M-p.
\]
Since \(2p\leq M\), we have \(p\leq M-p=d\). In particular, because a prime is at least \(2\),
\[
d\geq p\geq2.
\]
Also \(d\leq M\).

Suppose for contradiction that \(d\) is not prime. Because \(d\geq2\), it is then composite. Let \(q\) be its least prime factor. A standard least-factor argument gives
\[
q^2\leq d.
\]
For completeness, if \(d=qu\), minimality of \(q\) implies that every prime factor of \(u\) is at least \(q\); as \(u>1\) when \(d\) is composite and \(q\) is its least prime factor, one has \(u\geq q\), and hence \(d=qu\geq q^2\). Therefore
\[
q\leq\lfloor\sqrt d\rfloor.
\]
Since \(d\leq M\), monotonicity of the square root gives
\[
q\leq\lfloor\sqrt d\rfloor\leq\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor=r.
\]
Thus \(q\) is one of the small primes appearing in the defining condition for \(GB(M)\).

On the other hand, \(q\mid d=M-p\). Hence
\[
p\equiv M\pmod q,
\]
contradicting the defining requirement that \(p\not\equiv M\pmod q\) for every prime \(q\leq r\). This contradiction proves that \(d=M-p\) is prime. \(\square\)

We next record how the hypothesis \(a(n)\ne1\) supplies an associated prime. If \(GB(2n)\) were empty, then by the empty-product convention we would have
\[
a(n)=\prod_{p\in GB(2n)}p=1.
\]
Therefore
\[
a(n)\ne1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad GB(2n)\ne\varnothing.
\]
No converse is needed for the argument.

We can now prove the global implication to Goldbach's conjecture. Assume that
\[
a(k)\ne1\qquad\text{for every integer }k\geq3.
\]
Let \(n\geq3\) be arbitrary and put \(M=2n\). The hypothesis gives \(a(n)\ne1\), so \(GB(M)\) is nonempty. Choose any \(p\in GB(M)\). By definition, \(p\) is prime. By the lemma, its complement
\[
p_2=M-p=2n-p
\]
is also prime. Moreover, membership in \(GB(M)\) gives \(p\leq M/2\), in particular \(p\leq M\), so subtraction involves no truncation and
\[
p+(M-p)=M=2n.
\]
Thus \(2n\) is the sum of the two primes \(p\) and \(2n-p\). Since \(n\geq3\) was arbitrary, every even integer \(2n>2\) in the stated range is a sum of two primes. This is Goldbach's conjecture in the formulation used here.

Finally, we prove the more specific local assertion involving the maximum Goldbach-associated prime. Fix \(n\geq3\) and suppose only that \(a(n)\ne1\). As above, the finite set \(GB(2n)\) is nonempty. Every nonempty finite set of natural numbers has a maximum, so define
\[
m=\max GB(2n).
\]
Then
\[
m\in GB(2n)
\]
and, by the defining property of a maximum,
\[
k\leq m\qquad\text{for every }k\in GB(2n).
\]
Because \(m\in GB(2n)\), the number \(m\) is prime and \(m\leq(2n)/2=n\). Applying the lemma with \(M=2n\) and \(p=m\) shows that
\[
2n-m
\]
is prime. The inequality \(m\leq2n\) ensures that
\[
(2n-m)+m=2n.
\]
Consequently
\[
(2n-m,m)
\]
is a Goldbach partition of \(2n\), with \(m\) specifically the largest member of \(GB(2n)\). This establishes both the existence and maximality assertions for \(m\), the primality of its complement, and the claimed Goldbach partition.
